content:
Energy flow in ecosystems is a fundamental ecological concept that describes how energy from the sun is captured by producers and then transferred through various trophic (feeding) levels in an ecosystem. Unlike nutrients, which can be recycled, energy flows in a one-way direction through ecosystems, with significant losses at each transfer.
 The process begins with photosynthesis, where primary producers (mainly green plants, algae, and certain bacteria) convert solar energy into chemical energy stored in organic compounds like glucose. This transformation captures only about 1-2% of the available solar energy, but it forms the energetic foundation for virtually all life on Earth. Primary producers not only sustain themselves with this energy but also provide the energy source for all other organisms in the ecosystem.
 Consumers obtain energy by feeding on other organisms. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat producers, secondary consumers (carnivores) eat herbivores, and tertiary consumers (top predators) eat secondary consumers. Omnivores consume organisms from multiple trophic levels. Decomposers and detritivores, including fungi, bacteria, and certain invertebrates, break down dead organic matter and waste products, recycling nutrients back into the ecosystem while obtaining energy for their own needs.
 A critical concept in ecosystem energy flow is ecological efficiencyâthe percentage of energy transferred from one trophic level to the next. Following the Second Law of Thermodynamics, each energy transfer is inefficient. Typically, only about 10% of the energy available at one trophic level is converted to biomass at the next level. The rest is lost as heat through respiration, or remains unconsumed or undigested. This inefficiency creates what ecologists call the "10% rule" and explains why energy pyramids are always upright, with producers forming a broad base and each successive trophic level containing fewer individuals and less total energy.
 Food chains depict linear energy transfer relationships between organisms, while food webs illustrate the complex interconnected feeding relationships in an ecosystem. These structures help ecologists understand energy dynamics and predict how changes in one population might affect others. Biomass, the total mass of living organisms in an ecosystem, is another way to measure stored energy at each trophic level, and like energy, typically decreases at higher trophic levels.

scenario.title: EcoTray: Cafeteria Energy Flow
scenario.content: Students manage a virtual school cafeteria where lunch trays represent ecosystems and food items represent different organisms. The simulation begins with 'producer' items (plants) that capture energy from the sun, which then transfer energy to primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), and decomposers. Students observe how energy decreases at each trophic level through smaller portion sizes. They experiment with different ecosystem compositions by arranging various food combinations on trays, observing how changes in one population affect energy availability throughout the system. Challenges include maintaining ecosystem balance when certain species are removed or environmental conditions change.

hypothesis.description: Students will be able to describe the unidirectional flow of energy through ecosystems from producers to various consumer levels, identify the role of different organisms in energy transfer, and explain why energy availability decreases at each successive trophic level according to the 10% rule.
